name: Cardiac embryology is often presented as isolated stages, yet understanding congenital heart defects (CHDs) requires knowing the developmental process and where it goes wrong. Medical students memorise outcomes instead of understanding the root cause.
text: Cardiac embryology is often presented as isolated stages, yet understanding congenital heart defects (CHDs) requires knowing the developmental process and where it goes wrong. Medical students memorise outcomes instead of understanding the root cause.

Congenital heart defects (CHDs) are the most common category of birth defect, affecting roughly 1 in 100 live births, and they remain one of the hardest topics in the medical curriculum to teach well. The reason is structural: almost every CHD is best understood not as a static anatomical abnormality, but as a point of arrest or misdirection in a dynamic developmental sequence
Textbook diagrams and atlases are accurate and well-illustrated but inherently static — a learner has to bridge the gap between discrete stages themselves.

 Cadaveric or pathology specimens are the gold standard for realism but are scarce, especially at embryonic stages, and can't be manipulated or reset.

Physical 3D-printed models allow handling but are typically limited to one or two fixed developmental stages, since printing a full sequence is costly and each model is static once made.

Congenital heart defects (CHDs) are the most common category of birth defect, affecting roughly 1 in 100 live births, and they remain one of the hardest topics in the medical curriculum to teach well. The reason is structural: almost every CHD is best understood not as a static anatomical abnormality, but as a point of arrest or misdirection in a dynamic developmental sequence
Textbook diagrams and atlases are accurate and well-illustrated but inherently static — a learner has to bridge the gap between discrete stages themselves.

 Cadaveric or pathology specimens are the gold standard for realism but are scarce, especially at embryonic stages, and can't be manipulated or reset.

Physical 3D-printed models allow handling but are typically limited to one or two fixed developmental stages, since printing a full sequence is costly and each model is static once made.

My primary audience is pre-clinical medical students learning cardiac embryology. Looking at student discussions, I identified three recurring struggles: visualising development, memorising without fully understanding, and forgetting concepts after exams. A 2026 study also found that nearly 78% of surveyed students felt additional resources would have improved their understanding.

name: Comparing normal and abnormal anatomy helps explain how developmental variation can produce congenital defects.

Apple Vision Pro is a wearable computer that places digital 3D content in the learner’s room. It places digital objects into the learner’s environment. A student can bring the heart closer, rotate it, look behind it, and separate layers with their eyes and hands. That matters because the learning problem is spatial. The device is doing educational work here, not simply adding novelty.

text: Two learning paths share one interactive heart. Guided Learning introduces the concepts. Free Exploration allows learners to investigate and reinforce them.

I am designing first for medical students in pre-clinical training because they must connect embryology to later anatomy and congenital defects. HeartV0 offers two paths. Guided Learning explains the sequence, while Free Exploration lets students investigate the same anatomy independently.

Guided Learning breaks the content into 51 short steps across ten developmental stages and six congenital anomalies. As the explanation advances, the model changes focus and the app remembers progress. The learner still manipulates the heart rather than watching passively.

Free Exploration lets learners move across eight timeline stops or browse congenital anomalies. They can select, isolate, cut away, separate, or compare structures. The current prototype switches between discrete models. Continuous animated morphing is not built yet.

At the start, I had only the visionOS template and a concept. The current build now includes 16 interactive 3D models, 355 selectable parts, guided narration and captions, progress tracking, and a movable close-up window. My latest update rebuilt the visual finish across all 16 models with warmer tissue materials and studio lighting.

name: HeartV0 turns a sequence students usually have to imagine into something they can inspect, compare, and explain.
text: HeartV0 turns a sequence students usually have to imagine into something they can inspect, compare, and explain.

This prototype is deliberately honest about its limits. The models are enlarged educational illustrations, not scans or clinically validated anatomy. They do not simulate flow, pressure, contraction, or continuous morphing. Next, I would seek expert review, test comfort and usability, then measure comprehension and retention with medical students. The goal is evidence that spatial interaction helps learners understand and remember the sequence.
